title: Angle K-Means
claim: A simple geometric argument shows how angular relationships let us rule out many candidates that triangle-inequality pruning alone cannot.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, progressively shaded exclusion regions on circle diagrams
description: Three side-by-side circular geometry diagrams share the same notation: red dots mark the origin o, the current center c_g, the sample x_i and a candidate center c_j. Panel (a), 'Triangle inequality', shows a large empty circle of radius 2r_i around c_g, with labeled segments r_i, 2r_i and ||c_g − c_j||₂ < 2r_i. Panel (b), 'Two special cases', adds smaller circles around x_i and its mirror x̂_i. A purple wedge and a green annular sector below c_g are the regions where a center cannot beat the current one. Red arcs mark the angles β_i and θ_gj. Panel (c), 'Angle k-means', fills the large circle with blue except for the two small circles, showing the full region where distance computation can be skipped. The eye goes first to the colored regions, and the blue area in (c) is the biggest.
caption: xi represents the sample that is ready to update its assignment, cg denotes the center previously assigned to xi, o represents the origin of coordinates. (a): According to the triangle inequality, if ∥xi −cj∥2 < ri, then ∥cg −cj∥2 must be less than 2ri, so we only need to consider the center whose distance from cg is less than 2ri. (b): Two special cases of Angle k-means: If the centers are located in the cyan or purple areas, then the distance from them to xi must be greater than or equal to ri. (c): Angle k-means: if cos(βi −θgj) ≤∥cg −cj∥2/(2ri), i.e., cj is located in the blue area, then we have ∥xi −cj∥2 ≥ri. So there is no need to calculate the distance between xi and cj.
abstract: We propose an accelerated exact $k$-means algorithm, Angle $k$-means. As its name suggests, the algorithm mainly leverages angular relationships between data points and cluster centers to reduce computational overhead. Although grounded in straightforward geometric principles, it delivers substantial performance improvements in empirical evaluations. In contrast to existing acceleration techniques, our model introduces no new hyperparameters, preserving full compatibility with standard $k$-means. Theoretical analysis shows that Angle $k$-means maintains linear time complexity with respect to both sample size and dimensionality, while empirical evaluations on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate significant speedup over state-of-the-art algorithms such as ball $k$-means and Exp-ns.
